section.heading: 5.5. The Substitution Rule
section.paragraph: Because of the Fundamental Theorem, it’s important to be able to find antiderivatives. But our antidifferentiation formulas don’t tell us how to evaluate integrals such as
$$\int{2x\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}\mathit{dx}}$$
To find this integral we use the problem-solving strategy of introducing something extra. Here the “something extra” is a new variable; we change from the variable $$x$$ to a new variable $$u$$ .
section.heading: Substitution: Indefinite Integrals
section.paragraph: Suppose that we let $$u$$ be the quantity under the root sign in (1), $$u = 1 + x^{2}$$ . Then the differential of $$u$$ is $$\mathit{du} = 2x\mathit{dx}$$ . Notice that if the $$\mathit{dx}$$ in the notation for an integral were to be interpreted as a differential, then the differential $$2x\mathit{dx}$$ would occur in (1) and so, formally, without justifying our calculation, we could write

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{2x\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}2x\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{\sqrt{u}\mathit{du}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{2x\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{2}{3}u^{3 \slash 2} + C = \frac{2}{3}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2} + C} \end{array}$$
Differentials were defined in Section 3.10. If $$u = f(x)$$ , then
$$\mathit{du} = f^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}$$
But now we can check that we have the correct answer by using the Chain Rule to differentiate the final function of Equation 2:
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2} + C} \right\rbrack = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{2}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{1 \slash 2} \cdot 2x = 2x\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}$$
In general, this method works whenever we have an integral that we can write in the form $$\int{f\left( {g(x)} \right)g^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ . Observe that if $$F^{\prime} = f$$ , then
$$\int{F^{\prime}\left( {g(x)} \right)g^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx} = F\left( {g(x)} \right) + C}$$
because, by the Chain Rule,
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {F\left( {g(x)} \right)} \right\rbrack = F^{\prime}\left( {g(x)} \right)g^{\prime}(x)$$
If we make the “change of variable” or “substitution” $$u = g(x)$$ , then from Equation 3 we have
$${\int{F^{\prime}\left( {g(x)} \right)g^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}}} = F\left( {g(x)} \right) + C = F(u) + C = {\int{F^{\prime}(u)\mathit{du}}}$$
or, writing $$F^{\prime} = f$$ , we get
$${\int{f\left( {g(x)} \right)g^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{f(u)\mathit{du}}}$$
Thus we have proved the following rule.

section.paragraph: Notice that the Substitution Rule for integration was proved using the Chain Rule for differentiation. Notice also that if $$u = g(x)$$ , then $$\mathit{du} = g^{\prime}(x)\mathit{dx}$$ , so a way to remember the Substitution Rule is to think of $$\mathit{dx}$$ and $$\mathit{du}$$ in (4) as differentials.
Thus the Substitution Rule says: It is permissible to operate with $$\mathbf{dx}$$ and $$\mathbf{du}$$ after integral signs as if they were differentials.

section.paragraph: The idea behind the Substitution Rule is to replace a relatively complicated integral by a simpler integral. This is accomplished by changing from the original variable $$x$$ to a new variable $$u$$ that is a function of $$x$$ . Thus in Example 1 we replaced the integral $$\int{x^{3}\cos{({x^{4} + 2})}\mathit{dx}}$$ by the simpler integral $$\frac{1}{4}{\int{\cos u\mathit{du}}}$$ .

The main challenge in using the Substitution Rule is to think of an appropriate substitution. You should try to choose $$u$$ to be some function in the integrand whose differential also occurs (except for a constant factor). This was the case in Example 1. If that is not possible, try choosing $$u$$ to be some complicated part of the integrand (perhaps the inner function in a composite function). Finding the right substitution is a bit of an art. It’s not unusual to guess wrong; if your first guess doesn’t work, try another substitution.

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{x^{3}\cos{({x^{4} + 2})}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{\cos{({x^{4} + 2})} \cdot x^{3}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{4}{\int{\cos{({x^{4} + 2})} \cdot {({4x^{3}})}\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x^{3}\cos{({x^{4} + 2})}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{4}{\int{\cos{({x^{4} + 2})} \cdot \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({x^{4} + 2})}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{4}\sin{({x^{4} + 2})} + C} \end{array}$$
Similarly, the solution to Example 4 could be written like this:

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Solution An appropriate substitution becomes more apparent if we factor $$x^{5}$$ as $$x^{4} \cdot x$$ . Let $$u = 1 + x^{2}$$ . Then $$\mathit{du} = 2x\mathit{dx}$$ , so $$x\mathit{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\mathit{du}$$ . Also $$x^{2} = u - 1$$ , so $$x^{4} = \left( {u - 1} \right)^{2}$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{5}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{4} \cdot x\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{5}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int{\sqrt{u}{({u - 1})}^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\mathit{du}}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int{\sqrt{u}{({u^{2} - 2u + 1})}\mathit{du}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{5}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int{{({u^{5 \slash 2} - 2u^{3 \slash 2} + u^{1 \slash 2}})}\mathit{du}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{5}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{2}{7}u^{7 \slash 2} - 2 \cdot \frac{2}{5}u^{5 \slash 2} + \frac{2}{3}u^{3 \slash 2}} \right) + C} \\ {\phantom{\int{\sqrt{1 + x^{2}}x^{5}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{7}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{7 \slash 2} - \frac{2}{5}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{5 \slash 2} + \frac{1}{3}{({1 + x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2} + C} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Substitution: Definite Integrals
section.paragraph: When evaluating a definite integral by substitution, two methods are possible. One method is to evaluate the indefinite integral first and then use the Fundamental Theorem. For instance, using the result of Example 2, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \left. \int\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {2x + 1} \right)^{3 \slash 2}\rbrack_{0}^{4} = \frac{1}{3}(9)^{3 \slash 2} - \frac{1}{3}(1)^{3 \slash 2}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{\sqrt{2x + 1}\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {27 - 1} \right) = \frac{26}{3}} \end{array}$$
Another method, which is usually preferable, is to change the limits of integration when the variable is changed.

section.heading: Symmetry
section.paragraph: The next theorem uses the Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals (6) to simplify the calculation of integrals of functions that possess symmetry properties.

list.item: (a) If $$f$$ is even $$\left\lbrack {f( - x) = f(x)} \right\rbrack$$ , then $${\int_{- a}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx} = 2}}{\int_{0}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}}$$ .
(b) If $$f$$ is odd $$\left\lbrack {f( - x) = - f(x)} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$\int_{- a}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx} = 0}$$ .

In the first integral on the far right side we make the substitution $$u = - x$$ . Then $$\mathit{du} = - \mathit{dx}$$ and when $$x = - a$$ , $$u = a$$ . Therefore

list.item: (a) If $$f$$ is even, then $$f\left( {- u} \right) = f(u)$$ so Equation 9 gives $${\int_{- a}^{a}{f{(x)}\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{0}^{a}{f(u)\mathit{du}}} + {\int_{0}^{a}{f{(x)}\mathit{dx}}} = 2{\int_{0}^{a}{f{(x)}\mathit{dx}}}$$
(b) If $$f$$ is odd, then $$f\left( {- u} \right) = - f(u)$$ and so Equation 9 gives $${\int_{- a}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}} = - {\int_{0}^{a}{f(u)\mathit{du}}} + {\int_{0}^{a}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}} = 0$$

section.paragraph: Theorem 7 is illustrated by Figure 3. For the case where $$f$$ is positive and even, part (a) says that the area under $$y = f(x)$$ from $$- a$$ to $$a$$ is twice the area from $$0$$ to $$a$$ because of symmetry. Recall that an integral $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ can be expressed as the area above the $$x$$ -axis and below $$y = f(x)$$ minus the area below the axis and above the curve. So part (b) says the integral is $$0$$ because the areas cancel.
